title: Han dynasty
summary: The Han dynasty ruled a unified Chinese empire from 206 BCE to 220 CE, first from Chang'an and, after Wang Mang's Xin interregnum (9–23 CE), from Luoyang. Its census of 2 CE registered about 59.6 million people.
card: After the Qin empire broke apart in civil war, Liu Bang founded the Han, which held the Qin unification together for four centuries. Under Emperor Wu it pushed into Central Asia, Korea and the far south, while envoys such as Zhang Qian opened the routes later called the Silk Roads. Rebellion from 184 CE emptied the throne of real power, and the last emperor abdicated to Cao Pi of Wei in 220.
what:
The Han dynasty (漢 Hàn) was the ruling house of the Chinese empire for most of the four centuries after the Qin collapse. Liu Bang, a rebel commander, entered the Qin heartland in the first year of his reckoning (206 BCE), was made King of Han over Ba, Shu and Hanzhong by Xiang Yu, defeated Xiang Yu, and took the imperial title in 202 BCE. His capital, Chang'an in present-day Shaanxi, grew into a planned city with palaces, residential wards and two markets.

The Western (Former) Han reached its widest extent under Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE), who fought the Xiongnu steppe empire, sent Zhang Qian west to look for allies, retook southern China and northern Vietnam, founded commanderies in Korea, and in 101 BCE conquered Ferghana. A register compiled for 2 CE counted 103 commanderies and kingdoms, 1,314 counties, 12,233,062 households and 59,594,978 people.

Feuding factions, among them the families of imperial consorts, weakened the Western Han. In 9 CE Wang Mang, who had governed as acting emperor, dropped the Han name and proclaimed his own Xin dynasty; he was killed when rebel troops stormed the palace at Chang'an in 23 CE. Liu Xiu, a ninth-generation descendant of Liu Bang, took the throne in 25 CE as Emperor Guangwu and made Luoyang his capital, opening the Eastern (Later) Han. Ban Chao restored Han power in Central Asia between 73 and 94 CE, and in 105 CE the court eunuch Cai Lun presented an improved method of making paper.

After 168 CE, struggles between palace eunuchs and the great families weakened the court. In 184 CE Zhang Jue's Yellow Turban followers rose on a single day, and in 216 the general Cao Cao raised himself to King of Wei. The last emperor, Liu Xie (Emperor Xian), abdicated in favour of Cao Cao's son Cao Pi in 220 CE, and the empire divided among Wei, Shu-Han and Wu.

Sources disagree on where to put the dynasty's start and end: museum and teaching timelines begin it in 206 BCE, when Liu Bang's reign years start, others at his enthronement in 202 BCE, and Michael Loewe treats the revolt of 184 CE rather than the abdication of 220 as the real end of Han imperial authority.

uncertainty.note: Start: 206 BCE (astronomical -205) is the conventional date (Met, Columbia), the first year of Liu Bang's reckoning in the Hanshu; he took the imperial title in his fifth year, 202 BCE (-201). The Hanshu year 1 opens with the tenth month, because the Qin-style year began in the tenth month, so its first months fall before January of 206 BCE. End: formal abdication in 220 CE; Loewe treats the Yellow Turban revolt of 184 CE as the effective end of imperial authority. The Xin interregnum (9–23 CE) and the civil war to 25 CE fall inside the span but were not Han rule.

Polygons are to be drawn from the CHGIS V6 time-series prefecture (commandery) polygons, which cover 221 BCE onward but, by the dataset's own description, still have gaps before 1350 CE. Reference snapshots follow the Cambridge History of China maps of the Han empire in 143 BCE, 108 BCE, 2 CE and 140 CE. The Hanshu register of 2 CE gives the empire's extent as 9,302 li east to west and 13,368 li north to south, with 103 commanderies and kingdoms.

how: The Han grew out of the civil war that followed the First Emperor's death in 210 BCE. Liu Bang reached the Qin capital region first, accepted the surrender of the last Qin ruler, was assigned the kingdom of Han in the southwest by Xiang Yu, and then fought Xiang Yu for the whole realm, taking the imperial title in 202 BCE. The dynasty held the boundaries Qin had set and governed through commanderies and counties together with subordinate kingdoms and marquisates, all four of which the register of 2 CE still lists. Emperor Wu made Confucian learning the basis of official conduct and education, so the bureaucracy came to rely on men trained in the classics. Against the Xiongnu he sent armies north and envoys west: Zhang Qian, setting out with over a hundred men during the Jianyuan era (140–134 BCE), returned about thirteen years later with only two, but with knowledge of Ferghana, Sogdiana and Bactria. Posthouses and beacon towers along the Hexi Corridor and the conquest of Ferghana in 101 BCE gave the Han control of routes around the Taklamakan, and the Ferghana campaign brought in prized cavalry horses, while silk and gold went west in exchange for wine, spices, woollens, grapes, pomegranates and alfalfa. The Western Han weakened as factions, including consort families, fought for power, and Wang Mang, after ruling as acting emperor, took the throne in 9 CE. After his death in 23 CE, Liu Xiu restored the house at Luoyang. In the second century, rivalry between eunuchs and leading families divided the court after Emperor Huan died without a designated heir in 168. The Yellow Turban rising of 184, whose organised followers the Hou Hanshu puts at 360,000, prompted the court to put He Jin in command of the armies; Loewe sees this revolt as the end of real imperial authority. In the years that followed, the general Cao Cao rose to be King of Wei in 216, and his son Cao Pi received the abdication in 220.
why_it_matters: The Han turned the short-lived Qin unification into a lasting form of state. Its borders, inherited from Qin and held for four centuries, roughly outline the China of later history, and Michael Loewe notes that the centralised imperial model it created went largely unchallenged for some two thousand years, until the late nineteenth century. Several of its institutions outlived it directly. Emperor Wu's choice of Confucian learning as the basis of official conduct and schooling shaped the training of Chinese officials for many centuries, and Sima Qian's Shiji set the model for the official dynastic histories, including the Hanshu and Hou Hanshu used in this record. Its register of 2 CE, preserved commandery by commandery in the Hanshu, records nearly 60 million registered people in over 12 million households. Han envoys, the Ferghana campaign and the relay posts of the Hexi Corridor helped the long-distance exchange that UNESCO says grew sharply from the 2nd century BCE, carrying Chinese silk west and bringing grapes and alfalfa east. Paper, made in a cruder form in the Western Han and improved in the method Cai Lun presented in 105 CE, came into general use in the empire, according to the Hou Hanshu. A counterfactual shows what was at stake: had the civil war after 210 BCE ended in lasting division among rival kings, as Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE proposed, the idea of a single Chinese empire might never have hardened into the norm. The Han's collapse after 184 CE, and the division into rival kingdoms that followed, show how much that unity depended on the dynasty holding together.

related.title: Qin dynasty

perspectives.holder: Metropolitan Museum of Art; Columbia University Asia for Educators; Hanshu reign-year reckoning
perspectives.account: The dynasty begins in 206 BCE, the first year of Liu Bang's reign count, when he took the Qin heartland and was made King of Han.

perspectives.holder: Dating by imperial enthronement (Hanshu, Annals of Gaozu)
perspectives.account: Liu Bang became emperor only in his fifth year, 202 BCE, after defeating Xiang Yu; on this reading Han rule over a unified empire starts then.

perspectives.holder: Michael Loewe, Cambridge History of China vol. 1 (1986)
perspectives.account: The formal end is Emperor Xian's abdication in 220 CE, but imperial authority had in effect collapsed with the Yellow Turban revolt of 184 CE, leaving a powerless emperor on the throne.

perspectives.holder: Hou Hanshu (5th century CE), the traditional account
perspectives.account: Cai Lun devised paper from bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets and presented it in 105 CE; the empire called it 'Marquis Cai's paper'.

perspectives.holder: Archaeological finds: Fangmatan tomb 5 (Gansu) and Western Han sites; Li Xiaocen (2016), with doubts from Chen Gang
perspectives.account: Paper was already used in the Western Han, roughly 250 years before Cai Lun, who improved rather than invented it; whether the Fangmatan fragment counts as true paper is still debated.

perspectives.holder: Hans Bielenstein, Cambridge History of China vol. 1 (1986)
perspectives.account: Traditional histories judge Wang Mang through the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven as a usurper, which makes a fair assessment of his reign difficult.

numbers.label: Registered population of the empire (register of 2 CE, Hanshu Treatise on Geography)
numbers.note: Single figure as recorded in the Hanshu. It is a registered count, not a modern estimate of total population; the commandery entries are dated Yuanshi 2 (src-hanshu-28a). Secondary works also cite a lower total of about 57.7 million, but no source I opened gave or explained it, so it is not used here.

audience_note: Mentions war, rebellion and violent deaths (the killing of Wang Mang in 23 CE, frontier wars with the Xiongnu) without graphic description.

importance.justification: One of the largest states of the ancient world, ruling tens of millions of people for four centuries, it fixed the model of the unified Chinese empire and its official historiography, so it must be visible at whole-planet view.
